name: Toreando / Float Passing
keyCorrections: If they keep framing you: switch your passing angle to the opposite side
If they keep re-guarding: your posts are too shallow — pummel deeper into their hip line
If they keep attacking your legs: raise your hands and stay more upright
description: Toreando (float) passing is a modern no-gi passing system that uses constant lateral movement, hip switches, and hand posting to float around the opponent's guard rather than grinding through it. Popularized by the Ruotolo brothers and Nicky Ryan, float passing keeps the passer on their feet, using momentum and hip mobility to attack passing lanes as they open.
shortInstruction: Stay on your feet, keep your hips mobile, post on their legs to redirect their frames, and float to side control when they commit to a defensive direction.
summary: Float passing works by never settling into a static position. The passer uses continuous lateral movement, switching hips and posting on the opponent's legs to prevent them from establishing frames. Unlike pressure passing which locks chest-to-chest, float passing maintains distance until the moment of penetration. The key is to keep your head above their hips and use your hands to pummel their legs, creating passing windows through hip switches and angle changes.
whyItWorks: Constant movement prevents the opponent from locking their guard or establishing frames
Staying on your feet removes the threat of sweeps and leg locks from seated guard
Hip switches and posts create passing windows that don't exist in static passing
Float passing forces the opponent to constantly re-adjust — creating hesitation and openings
commonMistakes: Stopping movement after a successful post — float passing requires continuous motion
Dropping your head below their hips — exposes you to guillotines and front headlocks
Posting with straight arms — makes your posts weak and easy to swat away
Staying too long in one passing lane — the opponent will adjust their defense
Failing to switch direction after the opponent commits to defending one side
coachingCues: Keep moving — stop and you die in float passing
Head above hips at all times
Post, pivot, pummel — the three Ps of float passing
If they defend one side, switch to the other
Float over their frames, don't smash through them
safetySummary: Staying on your feet significantly reduces the risk of heel hooks and ankle locks
Be mindful of your head position to avoid guillotine counters
Float passing is safer than pressure passing against flexible guard players

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Float passing has 3 branches: Toreando Post → Hip Switch Backstep → Leg Drag Float

decisionTree.condition: Opponent frames on your near leg
decisionTree.action: Post on their far hip, switch your hips, and circle to the opposite side

decisionTree.condition: Opponent opens their guard to attack legs
decisionTree.action: Drop your hips, leg drag the near leg, and pass to side control
Snap their head down, circle behind, and take the back

moneyDetails: Float passing is the most effective passing system against flexible/inverted guard players
Mastering float passing combined with pressure passing gives you a complete no-gi passing game
The Ruotolos and Nicky Ryan have used float passing to dominate ADCC and IBJJF no-gi
fixItFast: If they keep framing: switch lanes — go to the opposite passing side
If they keep sweeping: your weight is too far forward — sit your hips back
If they keep attacking legs: stand taller and use hand posts to keep distance
